Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

assumption noun

something taken for granted

also on the assumption that, make an assumption, a false assumption

classical

Cic. Div. 1.118: hōc autem positō atque concessō

hōc positō

ablative absolute of pōnō

on this assumption, this being taken as given

Latin usually makes an assumption a verb: what one lays down (pōnere) or takes (sūmere) as given, with an accusative and infinitive (see assume). Positum sit, let it be taken as given (Cic. Or. 14, Lewis & Short).

Other words

  • sūmptiō, sūmptiōnis f. — an assumption, a premise (in an argument)

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Cic. Div. 2.108 (Lewis & Short)

    Cicero’s Latin for the logicians’ λήμματα; a word of argument, not of conversation (see premise).

  • opīniō, opīniōnis f. — a belief held without proof, a supposition

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Cic. Fragm. Scaur. 7: apud hominēs barbarōs opīniō plūs valet saepe quam rēs ipsa (Lewis & Short)

    An assumption in the sense of a belief that may be wrong (see opinion).

Examples

  • dēmus tibi istās duās sūmptiōnēs, ea quae λήμματα appellant dialecticī; sed nōs Latīnē loquī mālumus

    let us grant you those two assumptions, which the logicians call lemmata; but we prefer to speak LatinCic. Div. 2.108 (Lewis & Short)

  • hōc autem positō atque concessō

    but once this is assumed and grantedCic. Div. 1.118

See also assume, premise, suppose, opinion.
